This balanced approach helps ensure that our audit resources

address both traditional financial risks and emerging operational cybersecurity and student focus risk. The endorsed topics collectively represent a comprehensive view of risk across the division, and provide multiple options for selecting the final FY27 audit plan.

Next slide. An equally important part of the planning process involves deciding which topics should not move forward currently. I want to emphasize that deferred topics were not considered unimportant or low risk.

Rather, they were deferred for practical planning reasons related to timing, capacity, readiness, expertise, and audit sequencing. For any committee member interested in additional detail, the full rationale supporting each individual decision has been documented and is available upon request.

There were four primary reasons why 25 topics were not endorsed this year. First, limited audit capacity. With a three-person audit team, we must remain selective to ensure audits are completed thoroughly and in accordance with professional standards.

Second, specialized expertise. Some topics require technical capabilities or core co-sourced support that are not currently available. Third, data and trend readiness. Certain audits would be more meaningful after additional data becomes available or trends mature over time.

Lastly, scope and stakeholder readiness. Some topics require further definition, coordination, or stakeholder engagement before an audit can be conducted effectively. Importantly, deferred topics remain part of the audit universe and will be considered during future planning cycles.

This slide provides examples of how those factors influence special decisions. Capital projects was deferred primarily because of resource limitations and is already identified as a potential FY28 engagement. Oracle ERP implementation was deferred due to the need for specialized IT audit expertise and potentially outsourcing support.

Several workforce-related topics, including workforce capacity, succession planning, and enrollment forecasting, were deferred until additional data and organizational decisions provide a stronger audit foundation. Interdepartmental coordination and program evaluation require additional scope definition before fieldwork can produce meaningful results.

Finally, compensation equity and internal investigations require substantial stakeholder cooperation and data accessibility. Conducting those audits prematurely could result in incomplete findings and reduced audit value. These are examples that demonstrate the deferral decisions were strategic and practical rather than reflections of topic importance.
